sections.html:
Helena is Montana's capital and the seat of Lewis and Clark County. The 2020 census counted 32,091 residents in about 17 square miles, and the metro area, which covers Lewis and Clark and Jefferson counties, had 83,058 people. The city sits in the Helena Valley with Tenmile Creek running through it and hillside neighborhoods rising on the edges. Slopes, access roads and fire exposure are part of how a buyer sees a hillside lot.

Government anchors the local economy. Roughly 18 percent of working Helenans are employed by state agencies, and county, federal, school and health care jobs add to that. Buyers often have ties to government, education or medicine, and owners who relocate for work, retire or inherit from a parent usually want a predictable closing date. Older houses from the gold camp era give parts of town a Victorian look, so ask a buyer how they view an older home.

Helena is semi-arid, with long, cold winters, hot dry summers and an average of only 11.4 inches of precipitation a year, mostly in spring. Temperatures have ranged from 105 degrees Fahrenheit to minus 42. With swings that wide, expect a buyer's inspector to look closely at the roof, siding and foundation.

The city's zoning code says its regulations seek to minimize danger from wildland fires, stormwater flooding, soil erosion and other environmental hazards, to mitigate traffic hazards and to protect the scenic character of hillside areas. Chapter 2 of Title 11 of the Helena City Code sets out the land uses allowed in each district.

The same chapter covers accessory dwelling units. An ADU is allowed only with a single-dwelling unit residence, one per lot, and a detached or attached ADU cannot exceed 75 percent of the main house or 1,000 square feet, whichever is less. If your property has a garage apartment or a converted basement, check with the city that it was permitted and fits these limits, because an unpermitted unit has to be disclosed.

A simple checklist for a sale:

  • Confirm the zoning district of your lot on the city's planning pages.
  • Find permits for additions, finished basements and any second unit.
  • Note any hillside, drainage or access issues you know of.
  • Collect records for roof, furnace and chimney work.

The City of Helena's Community Development Department handles this. Its Building Division reviews building and site plans, issues building permits and does inspections within city limits, and Historic Preservation sits in the same department.

If you remodeled without permits, a buyer may ask the city for records, and a missing permit can slow a deal. Montana's disclosure law asks sellers to say whether substantial additions or alterations were made without a building permit. Deal with that before the contract rather than after.

sections.h2: How and when Helena property tax is paid
sections.html:
Lewis and Clark County collects the tax and processes about 37,000 real estate tax bills a year. The treasurer mails bills, usually in late October, and the first payment is due November 30 or within 30 days of the postmark, whichever is later. The second payment is due May 31.

Tax questionWhere to go
PaymentsLewis and Clark County, 316 North Park Avenue, Room 113, Helena
Property tax office phone406-447-8329
First half dueNovember 30, or 30 days after the postmark if later
Second half dueMay 31
ADU size limitOne per lot, up to 75% of the main house or 1,000 sq ft

At closing, the title company settles whatever tax is owed for the current period out of your proceeds.

sections.h2: What a Montana seller must disclose
sections.html:
You must give the buyer a written statement of adverse material facts you actually know. Section 70-20-502 of the Montana Code includes matters of title, water and wastewater, utilities, structural and mechanical systems, soil and drainage problems, and any testing for radon, mold, lead-based paint or contaminated soil. If the statement is delivered after a contract is signed, the buyer has three days to rescind under section 70-20-504.

Exemptions in section 70-20-503 include court-ordered transfers such as probate, foreclosure sales and transfers to a spouse, child or parent.

sections.h2: Your options if you need to sell a Helena house
sections.html:
• List with an agent. The house is exposed to the full market, with showings and a buyer's inspection and loan to work through.
  • Sell on your own. There is no commission, but you manage the buyer, the contract and the disclosure yourself.
  • Accept a cash offer. The buyer purchases as is, and there is no loan approval to wait on. The offer takes account of the condition of the house, so ask for it in writing and compare your net.

Whatever the route, request a payoff statement for your mortgage and any liens, and an estimate of closing costs, so you know what is left.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit record to sell my Helena house?
faqs.a: Montana's disclosure statement asks about additions made without a building permit. Contact the city's Building Division to check what is on file.

faqs.q: How many accessory dwelling units can I have on a Helena lot?
faqs.a: One. The city code allows one ADU per lot, accessory to a single-dwelling unit residence, and limits it to 75 percent of the main house or 1,000 square feet, whichever is less.

faqs.q: When are Lewis and Clark County property taxes due?
faqs.a: The first half is due on November 30, or within 30 days of the postmark if that is later. The second half is due May 31.

faqs.q: Is Helena in a wildfire area?
faqs.a: The city's zoning code says it seeks to minimize danger from wildland fires, so fire exposure is a planning concern, especially on hillsides. Ask your insurer and the city about your specific address.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Helena house that I inherited?
faqs.a: Yes, once the person with legal authority over the estate can sign. Transfers ordered by a probate court are exempt from the seller disclosure statement under section 70-20-503.
